nameStory: The "pill" in pill woodlouse comes from their amazing ability to roll into a perfect ball when threatened, just like a tiny pill! This defensive behavior has earned them many playful nicknames including "roly-poly" and "doodle bug." The name "woodlouse" reflects their preference for rotting wood and damp places, even though they're actually crustaceans related to shrimp and lobsters.
description: Common pill woodlouses are small, armored creatures that look like tiny gray tanks scuttling through your garden. These oval-shaped animals have segmented bodies covered in hard, overlapping plates that give them a distinctly armored appearance. They typically grow to about half an inch long and are most famous for their ability to roll into a tight ball when disturbed. Despite their name, they're not insects but crustaceans - more closely related to lobsters than beetles!

idTips.label: Ball-rolling ability
idTips.description: When touched, they instantly curl into a perfect sphere about the size of a small marble - smooth and hard to the touch, with no visible body parts

idTips.label: Segmented armor
idTips.description: Seven distinct overlapping plates across the back create visible lines, feeling hard and smooth like tiny plastic when gently touched

idTips.label: Color and pattern
idTips.description: Usually slate gray to dark gray, sometimes with yellowish spots or marbled patterns, occasionally solid black or even reddish-brown

idTips.label: Seven pairs of legs
idTips.description: When walking, you can see seven pairs of short legs moving in waves beneath the body - they move slowly and deliberately

idTips.label: Antennae
idTips.description: Two pairs of antennae on the head, with the outer pair being longer and more visible as they tap around while exploring

idTips.label: Size and shape
idTips.description: About half an inch long when stretched out, oval-shaped and noticeably convex (humped) on top, flat underneath

habitat: Look for pill woodlouses in damp, dark places throughout New England - under logs, rocks, leaf litter, and mulch in gardens, forests, and parks. They thrive in moist soil rich in decaying organic matter, from sea level to mountain elevations. You'll often find them congregating under flowerpots, compost piles, or anywhere the soil stays consistently moist.

seasonality.spring: Most active as temperatures warm and they emerge from winter hiding spots under deep leaf litter and logs. This is when you'll see them most often during the day.
seasonality.summer: Active throughout but tend to hide during hot, dry days. Best found in early morning or evening when they venture out to feed on decaying plant matter.
seasonality.fall: Very active as they feed heavily on falling leaves and prepare for winter. Often found in large groups under decomposing leaf piles.
seasonality.winter: Hidden deep under logs, rocks, or in basements and cellars where they remain sluggish but alive throughout New England's cold months.

funFact: Pill woodlouses are one of the few land animals that can drink through their rear end - they absorb water through special tubes in their tail area, which is why you'll often see them backing up to water drops!
confusionNotes: Often confused with pill millipedes, which also roll into balls but have many more body segments (usually 12+ versus 7) and shinier, more metallic-looking armor. Memory trick: "Lucky seven segments" for pill woodlouses versus "many more" for millipedes.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "bugs," these are actually crustaceans that breathe through gills and need moisture to survive - they're essentially land-dwelling relatives of lobsters and crabs. Many people don't realize they're beneficial garden helpers that break down dead plant material into rich soil.
compareHints: The Common Pill Woodlouse is distinguished from its relative the Nosy Pill Woodlouse by its more uniformly gray coloration and slightly larger size. Common pill woodlouses also roll into tighter, more perfect spheres, while other woodlouse species in New England (like sowbugs) cannot roll into balls at all and have more flattened bodies.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The nosy pill woodlouse is distinguished from its close relative, the common pill woodlouse, primarily by that prominent nose-like projection on its head.
